transcript: How often do new musicals like The Lost Boys open cold on Broadway? As in, no pre Broadway try out, no off Broadway run. Let's look at some notable examples and some statistics. Well, if we look again just at the last 26 years or so, some of the most financially successful examples of this include The Book of Mormon, Motown, MJ, and most recently, just in time. But then you have some musicals that, even if they weren't as financially lucrative, they still got nominated for Best Musical at the Tonys, including some like it hot, New York, New York, shuffle along, something rotten, nice work if you can get it, Xanadu, and a show called Swing! We also have a couple grey area ones where they did a workshop that was open to the public where they could test out the material in front of an audience, but it wasn't really a fully mounted production. Information about these workshops can be a little hard to find after the fact. But if I understand correctly, some examples of this include Smash, Good Vibrations, Mr. Saturday Night, and school of rock. The last two were, of course, also nominated for best musical. Another grey area here are musicals like KPOP and King Kong, which technically had pre Broadway runs, but by the time it got to Broadway, the material had been so completely rewritten from the ground up, it was functionally a new musical playing in front of an audience for the first time, and of course we had a decent slew of other musicals in the last 26 years or so that truly did open cold on Broadway and did not find a lot of success either financially or at the Tonys. Including, but not limited to Tarzan, women on the verge of A nervous breakdown, bullets over Broadway, Holler if Ya Hear Me, flying over sunset, and of course, most infamously of them all, Spider Man: Turn Off the dark. But what about the numbers? Because this is a response to a video where I was talking about how musicals that open cold on Broadway rarely win Best Musical these days. And a couple people very astutely pointed out that that observation might be skewed by the fact that there are just not as many musicals that open cold on Broadway. But from what I can tell, it is still proportionally a little under. There's gonna be some margin for error in these numbers, I'm sure they're not exact exact, but by my count, there were about 232 new musicals that opened on Broadway since 2000. And 28 of them opened cold, or 35 if you include those grey area ones that I mentioned before. That's about 12% or 15% respectively, versus the 1 in 25 or 4% that have one best musical. But then again, that's only the difference of about two winners. Like, if two more of these musicals had won, it would be about proportional, which is not that big of a difference for a sample size this small. So, yeah, maybe musicals that open cold aren't at quite as much of a disadvantage as I implied in my last video.
